title: The history of understanding landslides
tagline: From Coulomb's friction and cohesion to a daily landslide forecast: how people learned why slopes fail, and how to get out of the way.
intro: A slope stays up as long as the ground's strength beats the pull of gravity. In 1773 Coulomb put that strength into two numbers, friction and cohesion. In the 1920s Terzaghi showed how water in the ground takes strength away. Disasters such as Vaiont, Kedarnath, Malin and Wayanad taught the rest. India now maps its landslide-prone land and has begun to forecast landslides district by district.

eras.name: Friction, cohesion and water
eras.summary: Coulomb and Terzaghi explain what holds a slope up, and the first great slides are studied.

eras.name: Naming, measuring and hard lessons
eras.summary: Engineers learn to calculate a factor of safety, Varnes names the kinds of landslide, and Vaiont, Aberfan and Huascarán show what is at stake.

eras.name: Mapping and warning
eras.summary: India maps its landslide-prone land, loses many lives in the Himalaya and the Western Ghats, and starts a national forecast.

events.title: Coulomb: friction and cohesion
events.text: The French military engineer Coulomb presented an essay to the Academy of Sciences in 1773. It was printed in 1776. He said that soil resists sliding in two ways: friction between the grains, which grows with the weight pressing down, and cohesion, which holds them together even with no weight.
events.why: Every slope calculation since has started from Coulomb's two numbers: friction and cohesion.

events.title: Elm: a mountain undercut by quarrying
events.text: Villagers had been quarrying slate from the foot of a mountain face for years. On a wet Sunday about 10 million cubic metres of rock broke away and ran 2 km across the valley floor. About 115 people died. The geologist Albert Heim interviewed witnesses and wrote that the rock had flowed, almost like a liquid.
events.why: It is widely considered the first rock avalanche to be studied scientifically, and it showed that digging at the foot of a slope can bring it down.

events.title: The Frank Slide
events.text: At 4:10 in the morning about 110 million tonnes of limestone fell from Turtle Mountain onto the edge of the coal-mining town of Frank. Witnesses said it was over in about 100 seconds. Between 70 and 90 people are thought to have died. Local First Nations people had long called it the mountain that moves.
events.why: The mountain is now one of the most closely watched in the world, with dozens of sensors on its face.

events.title: The Swedish slip circle
events.who: Knut Petterson, Sven Hultin, Wolmar Fellenius
events.text: In March 1916 a new quay in Gothenburg harbour slid into the water. The engineers who studied it treated the sliding surface as part of a circle and worked out the turning forces on the soil above it. Wolmar Fellenius extended the method and used a factor of safety: the strength available divided by the force trying to move the slope.
events.why: It gave engineers a way to put a number on how close a slope is to failing.

events.title: Terzaghi: water carries part of the load
events.text: Karl Terzaghi showed that the water in the gaps between soil grains carries part of the weight above. Only what is left, the effective stress, presses the grains together and makes friction. He set this out from 1923 and in his 1925 book Erdbaumechanik.
events.why: It explains why rain causes landslides: water pressure in the ground rises, the grains are pressed together less, and friction falls.

events.title: Bishop's method of slices
events.text: Alan Bishop published a better way to use the slip circle. He cut the sliding mass into vertical slices, included the water pressure on the base of each one, and added up the forces to find the factor of safety.
events.why: Bishop's simplified method is still built into the slope software engineers use today.

events.title: The Vaiont dam disaster
events.text: At 10:39 at night about 260 million cubic metres of rock slid off Monte Toc into the new Vaiont reservoir. It pushed a wave over the top of the 262 m dam; estimates of its height above the crest range from 150 to 250 m. The water destroyed Longarone and nearby villages. About 2,000 people died; counts range from 1,917 to about 2,500. The dam itself is still standing.
events.why: Filling a reservoir had raised the water pressure inside an old landslide. The warnings were there and were not acted on.

events.title: Aberfan
events.text: A heap of coal-mine waste had been tipped on a hillside over a natural spring. After heavy rain it turned to slurry and flowed into the village at about 9:15 in the morning, burying a junior school. 144 people died, 116 of them children. The inquiry put the blame on the National Coal Board.
events.why: Britain passed a law on the safety of mine tips in 1969, and engineers everywhere learned to keep water out of loose heaps.

events.title: The Darjeeling and Sikkim rains
events.text: At the end of the monsoon it rained for four days without a break. About 1,000 mm fell in 52 hours at the peak. Hundreds of landslides, and by some accounts thousands, cut the hill roads, and the Teesta river carried away the Anderson Bridge. About 1,000 people are thought to have died.
events.why: It is still the event against which landslides in the eastern Himalaya are measured.

events.title: Huascarán buries Yungay
events.text: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake shook ice and rock loose from the north peak of Huascarán. Some 50 to 100 million cubic metres of debris swept down the valley at more than 280 km/h and buried the towns of Yungay and Ranrahirca. Estimates of the dead in the avalanche range from about 18,000 to 30,000.
events.why: It is the deadliest landslide in recorded history, and it was set off by an earthquake, not rain.

events.title: Varnes names the kinds of landslide
events.text: David Varnes of the US Geological Survey sorted slope movements by two things: how the material moves and what it is made of. His 1958 scheme had falls, slides and flows. In 1978 he added topples and lateral spreads, and split the material into rock, debris and earth. It built on earlier work such as C. F. S. Sharpe's 1938 book.
events.why: A rock fall, a debris flow and an earth slide need different defences, so a shared set of names matters.

events.title: Caine's rainfall threshold
events.text: Nel Caine gathered 73 reports from around the world of rain that had set off shallow landslides and debris flows. Plotting how hard it rained against how long it lasted, he drew a line under the points. Below the line, slopes mostly held. Above it, they could fail.
events.why: Rainfall thresholds like this one are the basis of most landslide warnings today.

events.title: The classification is updated
events.who: David Cruden, David Varnes; Oldrich Hungr, Serge Leroueil, Luciano Picarelli
events.text: David Cruden and David Varnes revised the scheme in 1996 and added a speed scale with seven classes, from extremely slow (less than 16 mm a year) to extremely rapid (more than 5 m a second). In 2014 Oldrich Hungr and colleagues updated it again, with 32 named types.
events.why: Speed decides whether people can walk away from a landslide, so it became part of the name.

events.title: Malpa
events.text: At about 3 in the morning a rock fall and debris wiped out the village of Malpa in the Kali valley, in what is now Uttarakhand. The toll is given as 221 people, among them about 60 pilgrims resting on the way to Kailash Mansarovar.
events.why: It showed how exposed pilgrim routes and night halts in the high Himalaya are.

events.title: GSI becomes India's nodal agency for landslides
events.text: The Government of India named the Geological Survey of India as the nodal agency for landslide studies. GSI estimates that about 0.42 million sq km, or 12.6% of India's land outside the snow-covered areas, is prone to landslides: the Himalaya, the hills of the North-East, the Western Ghats and Konkan, and part of the Eastern Ghats.
events.why: One agency became responsible for mapping, studying and later forecasting landslides across the country.

events.title: Sensors on a slope in Munnar
events.who: Maneesha V. Ramesh and team, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham
events.text: A team from Amrita University buried sensors for rain, soil moisture, water pressure and movement in a hillside above Munnar and linked them by radio and satellite to their campus. A pilot began in 2008. In July 2009, during very heavy rain, the system issued a warning that the Kerala government passed on. Amrita describes it as India's first wireless sensor network for landslides.
events.why: It measured the thing that matters most, water pressure inside the slope, in real time.

events.title: National guidelines on landslides
events.text: NDMA published its National Guidelines on the Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches. They cover hazard mapping, building rules, monitoring, warning and public awareness. On 27 September 2019 NDMA followed with a National Landslide Risk Management Strategy.
events.why: Landslides were treated as a risk to plan for in advance, not only an emergency to respond to.

events.title: Kedarnath and the Uttarakhand floods
events.text: The monsoon came early and very heavy rain fell on melting snow. Above Kedarnath the bank of loose glacial debris holding back Chorabari lake gave way, and water, mud and boulders swept through the temple town. Floods and landslides hit valleys across the state. More than 5,700 people were presumed dead according to the state government in July 2013, and later counts are above 6,000. More than 1 lakh people were evacuated.
events.why: It was India's worst mountain disaster in decades, and it led to new work on warnings and on building in river valleys.

events.title: India starts mapping every landslide-prone slope
events.text: GSI began the National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping programme in the 2014–15 field season. Its aim was to map all 0.42 million sq km of landslide-prone land at a scale of 1:50,000, sorted into high, moderate and low susceptibility. The government has since reported the mapping complete: about 4.3 lakh sq km in parts of 19 states and union territories.
events.why: The maps show where slopes are most likely to fail, which is the first thing planners need to know.

events.title: Malin
events.where: Malin, Ambegaon taluka, Pune district, Maharashtra
events.text: Early in the morning, after about 108 mm of rain the day before, a hillside slid onto the village of Malin in the Western Ghats. About 45 houses were buried and 151 people died. Geologists who studied the site pointed to the rain and also to the levelling of slopes for farming and the loss of trees.
events.why: It showed that the Western Ghats, not only the Himalaya, need landslide maps and warnings.

events.title: Kerala: two monsoons of landslides
events.where: Idukki, Wayanad and Malappuram districts, Kerala
events.text: In August 2018 Kerala had its worst floods since 1924. About 341 major landslides were reported from ten districts, and more than 480 people died in the floods and slides. On 8 August 2019 two hillsides failed within hours of each other: at Puthumala in Wayanad, where 17 people died, and at Kavalappara in Malappuram, where 59 died, including 11 who were never found.
events.why: Two years running showed that extreme rain on steep, altered slopes was becoming a regular danger in Kerala.

events.title: Counting the world's fatal landslides
events.who: Melanie Froude and David Petley; Dalia Kirschbaum and NASA
events.text: Melanie Froude and David Petley published a count of fatal landslides not caused by earthquakes from 2004 to 2016: 55,997 deaths in 4,862 events, most of them in Asia and most set off by rain. NASA has kept its own Global Landslide Catalog of rain-triggered landslides since 2007.
events.why: Landslides kill far more people than was once thought, and the databases show where and when.

events.title: Daily forecasts for Darjeeling and the Nilgiris
events.who: Geological Survey of India, British Geological Survey, King's College London and partners
events.where: Darjeeling, West Bengal, and the Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu
events.text: The LANDSLIP project, which ran from 2016 to 2022, joined rainfall forecasts to rainfall thresholds worked out for each kind of terrain. In the 2020 and 2021 monsoons GSI sent experimental daily landslide forecast bulletins to officials in two districts: Darjeeling and the Nilgiris.
events.why: It was the trial run for a national landslide forecast.

events.title: Pettimudi
events.where: Pettimudi, near Munnar, Idukki district, Kerala
events.text: Late at night, in extreme rain, debris from a slope near Eravikulam National Park came down a stream onto rows of tea-estate workers' homes. 66 bodies were recovered and 4 people were never found.
events.why: The people who died were plantation workers living in old quarters at the foot of a slope: where people live matters as much as the rain.

events.title: Joshimath sinks
events.text: Cracks opened in roads and in more than 800 buildings in the hill town of Joshimath, which stands on old landslide debris. Satellite measurements by ISRO's remote sensing centre showed the ground dropping about 5.4 cm in 12 days, between 27 December 2022 and 8 January 2023. Hundreds of families were moved out.
events.why: Not all slope failures are sudden: a slow one can still make a town unsafe.

events.title: The Landslide Atlas of India
events.text: ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre published an atlas built from satellite images: about 80,000 landslides mapped between 1998 and 2022. It ranked 147 districts in 17 states and 2 union territories by how exposed their people and property are. Rudraprayag in Uttarakhand came first. Wayanad in Kerala was 13th.
events.why: It turned 25 years of satellite pictures into a list of where the risk is greatest.

events.title: A national landslide forecasting centre
events.text: The National Landslide Forecasting Centre was inaugurated at GSI in Kolkata, with the Bhusanket web portal and the Bhooskhalan mobile app. Daily bulletins began for Kalimpong, Darjeeling and the Nilgiris. By the 2025 monsoon, experimental and operational bulletins covered 21 districts in 8 states. The aim is a warning system for all landslide-prone states by 2030.
events.why: India now forecasts landslides the way it forecasts weather, though so far only for some districts.

events.title: Wayanad: Mundakkai and Chooralmala
events.text: After about 570 mm of rain in two days, a hillside above Punjirimattom failed in the early hours. The debris ran down a river valley for several kilometres, through Mundakkai and Chooralmala, in at least two surges. The official count is 298 dead, which includes 32 missing people later declared dead. Some reports give higher figures.
events.why: It was the deadliest landslide in Kerala's history, in a district the 2023 atlas had already ranked 13th in the country.

people.name: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb
people.note: Described the strength of soil as friction plus cohesion, the starting point of every slope calculation.

people.name: Albert Heim
people.note: Studied the 1881 Elm disaster and saw that a fast rock avalanche flows, not just slides.

people.name: Karl Terzaghi
people.role: Civil engineer, founder of soil mechanics
people.note: Showed that water pressure in the ground reduces the stress that holds soil grains together.

people.name: Alan W. Bishop
people.note: Wrote the 1955 method of slices for the factor of safety, and later helped investigate Aberfan.

people.name: David J. Varnes
people.note: His 1958 and 1978 classifications gave the world a shared set of names for landslides.

people.name: Maneesha V. Ramesh
people.role: Engineer and professor, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham
people.note: Led the team that put a wireless sensor network on a slope at Munnar and later in Sikkim.

series.title: Lives lost in single landslides in India in this story
series.caption: Reported deaths in six landslides, each at one place. The 2013 Uttarakhand disaster is left out because most of its victims died in floods. Figures include people never found.

facts: About 12.6% of India's land outside the snow-covered areas, some 0.42 million sq km, is prone to landslides, by the Geological Survey of India's estimate.
Landslide speeds span a huge range: the standard scale runs from less than 16 mm a year to more than 5 m a second.
The Vaiont dam survived the 1963 disaster almost undamaged. The wave went over the top of it.
From 2004 to 2016, landslides not caused by earthquakes killed 55,997 people in 4,862 events around the world.
Satellites have mapped about 80,000 landslides in India between 1998 and 2022.
Witnesses said the Frank Slide of 1903 was over in about 100 seconds.
